Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

Preserving an obsolete train timetable offers historians a valuable window into the rhythms of everyday mobility. Beyond listing departures and arrivals, a timetable reveals which towns were connected, how frequently services ran, and how long journeys took, allowing scholars to reconstruct the practical geography of a region at a given moment. Patterns such as early-morning commuter trains, reduced Sunday services, or seasonal excursions suggest how work, leisure, and religious observance structured ordinary lives. Comparing successive editions can also trace broader changes, including suburban growth or rural decline. However, a timetable records planned rather than actual movement: it cannot confirm whether trains ran punctually, how crowded they were, or who travelled. Historians must therefore corroborate it with other evidence, such as passenger accounts, ticket records, or newspapers, to understand lived experience.

Preserved railway timetables, though obsolete for travelers, offer historians a structured record of everyday mobility. They reveal which towns were connected, how frequently services ran, and at what hours, allowing scholars to infer patterns of commuting, market travel, and leisure excursions. Delays, cancellations, overcrowding, and unofficial adjustments rarely appear, so historians must supplement timetables with diaries, newspapers, or operational records to understand how journeys were truly experienced and who was able to make them.

A siphon is a continuous, water-filled tube that carries water from one container to another. To start it, the tube must be filled so there is no air gap. Once flowing, gravity pulls the water down the longer, lower outlet side. That falling water creates a lower pressure in the top part of the tube, so atmospheric pressure on the source container helps push more water up and over the bend.

The outlet must be lower than the water surface in the source container because the downward pull on the outlet side must be greater than the lift needed on the source side. If the outlet is not lower, there is no net driving force to keep water moving.

If air enters the tube, it can break the continuous column of water. Then pressure is no longer transmitted through the whole tube, and the siphon slows or stops.

Just pick the split ones off and put them to some other use.

A siphon transfers water between two containers by utilizing gravity and atmospheric pressure to move liquid over an elevated barrier. The process begins when the tube is filled with water, creating a continuous column. Gravity pulls the water down the longer, descending leg of the tube toward the lower container. This downward movement creates a partial vacuum or reduced pressure at the top of the siphon. Atmospheric pressure pushing on the surface of the source water then forces more liquid up the shorter leg to fill this low-pressure zone, sustaining the flow.

The outlet must be positioned lower than the source water surface because the driving force is the weight difference between the water columns in the two legs. If the outlet were higher or level with the source, gravity would not pull the water down with sufficient force to overcome the upward lift required on the intake side. A siphon is a tube filled with liquid that carries water up over a barrier and down to a lower point. Once the tube is full, gravity pulls on the longer, descending column of water on the outlet side. As that water moves out, the liquid behind it is pushed along by atmospheric pressure on the source surface, and cohesion between water molecules keeps the column continuous, so more water follows through the high point.

The outlet must be lower than the source surface because flow depends on a difference in pressure and weight between the two sides. If the outlet is lower, the descending column produces a net pull that drives water forward. If the outlet is level with the source, the forces balance and flow stops. If it is higher, water runs backward.

Air interrupts the flow by breaking the continuous column. Air is compressible and far lighter than water, so an air pocket at the top removes the pull that transmits motion through the liquid. Water on both sides then drains back toward the containers, and the siphon must be refilled, or primed, to start again.

This is particularly important for vulnerable groups such as children, the elderly, or those who might feel uneasy about riding next to vehicles.

Protected bike lanes can also often be installed more quickly and at a lower cost than large-scale highway construction projects, making them a cost-effective investment in urban infrastructure.

As seen in Paris, which expanded its cycle paths by over 1,000 kilometers, bike trips nearly doubled (based on city counts) between 2019 and 2022. This shows that people will opt for bikes if they have connected and convenient and protected routes available. It's not just about having a few isolated lanes, but connected networks from home to school, work, stores, and transit.

While some may claim that bike lanes take away space from cars or parking, streets are a shared public space and should be designed to serve the needs of the community as a whole, not just cars. I now live in Toronto and no longer use Hydro Ottawa, but I want to warn other consumers about their alarming billing practices. 

I previously held an account for one year while renting a downtown apartment. When I moved back in with my parents to pursue an MA, I officially cancelled my account and paid all outstanding charges. 

Despite the cancellation, Hydro Ottawa continued siphoning payments from my separate bank account at random intervals for over a year. I repeatedly phoned customer service and sent proof of the withdrawals, but representatives insisted my account was closed and that no debits were occurring. 

The truth emerged only when my parents and I cross-referenced our utility bills: Hydro Ottawa had mistakenly linked my banking details to my parents’ billing number simply because I had mentioned moving home. My parents had not noticed because they frequently received overpayment refunds, making the credits seem normal. 

After hours on the phone and speaking with multiple representatives, a manager finally investigated, confirmed the error, and addressed it. Shockingly, they initially refused a refund and offered only an apology. 

I will never again provide banking details for automatic debit. Hydro Ottawa’s reckless handling of customers’ personal data should deeply concern everyone.
